sections.label: The opening
sections.line: A secret is a QR code and a link to a public key: the workflow, who already does this, and a shared format.
sections.para: Send a QR code and a link to my key; they encrypt to it and return a QR code carrying their key too, so one exchange makes it two-way, trusted once fingerprints are checked. Agents work the same way, with no server. The pieces are proven elsewhere; the combination is new. QRE1 is a good start.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Seven lines: a QR code and a key link, the sender's key, fingerprints, agents, no server, prior art, QRE1.
sections.para: That is all it takes now. The first message carries the sender's key, so it becomes two-way. A fingerprint check, once, makes it trusted. Agents get their own key pairs. Any channel can carry ciphertext. Others already use QR codes for certificates, keys, passkeys and wallets. QRE1 needs chunking, forward secrecy and an identity.

sections.label: From the experiment to a workflow
sections.line: From the experiment to a workflow: publish my key, they encrypt to it, a QR code back, check once, then two-way.
sections.para: In my memo: all I have to do now is send them a QR code and the link to my public key. My key goes on pki.sgit.ai with its fingerprint; their browser or agent encrypts and adds its own key; the code travels any way; I decrypt and check their fingerprint once.

sections.label: Agents in the loop
sections.line: Agents in the loop: an agent makes a key pair, fetches the target's key, and hands over an image.
sections.para: It solves giving a vault key to an agent session without pasting it in the clear: the session shows its public key as a QR code, I return the vault key encrypted to it, and only that session opens it. The person in the middle controls every message and reads none.

sections.label: Why QR codes and not text
sections.line: Why QR codes and not text: a blob of text is unusable; a QR code is an object people can move.
sections.para: A person can see it, drop it in a chat or page, and a browser or agent reads it with a library. Up to 2,953 bytes fits keys, certificates, a signed message or an infographic, and a code can always carry a link to the rest.

sections.label: Who else already does this
sections.line: Who already does this: health certificates, key checks, device linking, Threema, passkeys, wallets, provisioning.
sections.para: The EU COVID certificate used CBOR, COSE, zlib and Base45. Signal, WhatsApp and Matrix verify keys by QR. Signal's device linking is closest: a public key out, a provisioning message encrypted back. Threema even shows an encrypted key backup as a QR code. Quishing is the warning: the trust must come from a fingerprint.

sections.label: A format to share: QRE1
sections.line: QRE1, the experiment's frame, as our shared format, after three additions.
sections.para: One line: version, recipient key id, one-off X25519 key, nonce, ChaCha20-Poly1305 ciphertext, optional Ed25519 key and signature. It is close to the one envelope secrets.sgit.ai called for. Add chunking across codes, forward secrecy after the first exchange, and an identity on pki.sgit.ai; use a good decoder and base45.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Not a product yet; the fingerprint check is human; QR codes can be abused; 2.9 KB a code; a sample of prior art.
sections.para: The workflow is a proposal from one afternoon's experiment. Without a fingerprint check a key proves nothing about its holder. A reader should show what a code holds before acting. Larger payloads need several codes or a link. The prior art is what could be verified from documentation.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: My voice memo, the QR experiment and its debriefs, and the specifications and documentation of the prior art.
sections.para: The memo of 21 October 2026; the experiment's two debriefs and QRE1; the eHealth Network certificate spec, RFC 9285, Signal, WhatsApp's whitepaper, Matrix, Signal-Server, Threema, FIDO CTAP 2.2, Sparrow and Blockchain Commons, the NCSC and Google Threat Intelligence; related articles on secrets, agents and keys.
